sources.title: A model guide for the GPT-6 family
sources.text: Practical tips for getting the best results from GPT‑6 models while managing time and cost GPT‑6 is our most advanced suite of models yet , and offers you a choice of models for different kinds of work. Whether you’re turning an idea into a working prototype, building and testing a feature, or orchestrating multi-step workflows across code repositories, databases, and external APIs, this guide explains how to choose a GPT‑6 model, give it effective instructions, manage long-running work, and prepare for production. Our most intelligent model for the best results. Near-Astra intelligence for a fifth of the price. Fast and efficient everyday work at scale. Run effectively in production. Use caching ⁠ (opens in a new window) and compaction ⁠ (opens in a new window) to manage context and cost. Measure task success and latency, and plan for monitoring and data controls. Match the model to your workload. Balance capability, cost, and latency by choosing the model, reasoning effort ⁠ (opens in a new window) , and speed that fit the task. Adjust your prompts and skills. Keep prompts, skills, and repository instructions consistent about what the model should deliver, what it can do independently, and what counts as done. Keep long-running work on track. Use steering ⁠ (opens in a new window) , async tools ⁠ (opens in a new window) , and delegation ⁠ (opens in a new window) to handle updates and independent work. Set clear boundaries for when the model should ask for input. Before deploying, there are several checks and best practices you’ll want to put into place. Keep efficiency in mind. Cut context the task doesn’t need ⁠ (opens in a new window) while keeping the evidence it does. Where your application supports it, run independent tasks together ⁠ (opens in a new window) so one slow step doesn’t hold up unrelated work. Reuse shared context through prompt caching ⁠ (opens in a new window) for recurring work. Cached input tokens cost up to 95% less ⁠ (opens in a new window) than uncached input tokens, depending on the model. Put stable instructions and reference material before changing task details, and keep tool definitions consistent. The caching dashboard ⁠ (opens in a new window) and diagnostics guide ⁠ (opens in a new window) help you see where that reuse breaks down. Include cache writes and any long-context rates when estimating the cost of a complete workflow. For longer conversations, compaction ⁠ (opens in a new window) reduces context size while preserving the state needed to continue. Decide how you’ll monitor behavior ⁠ (opens in a new window) and review the data controls ⁠ (opens in a new window) for your application. Test before deploying: Run representative tasks and measure task success, latency, and cost per successful task. Check out our API deployment checklist ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Think of the model choice and reasoning level as an intelligence/price tradeoff. GPT‑6 Astra ⁠ (opens in a new window) for the hardest reasoning work where maximum intelligence is needed. GPT‑6.1 Sol ⁠ (opens in a new window) for complex coding, research, and computer use. GPT‑6 Luna ⁠ (opens in a new window) for focused tasks at scale and everyday, repeated work with a clear goal, such as extracting invoice fields, classifying requests, or producing structured summaries. When evaluating the best model for the task, compare pricing ⁠ (opens in a new window) for each model. Reasoning level: In the API, choose how much effort the model spends on the task. Low: Routine tasks, such as extracting facts or making small edits. Medium: Work requiring judgment, such as planning a feature or comparing options. High: Difficult debugging, deeper analysis, or careful review. Extra high / Max: Test where supported when High falls short, and keep only if the improvement justifies the added time and cost. In the API, you can change reasoning effort mid-conversation ⁠ (opens in a new window) without breaking cache. In Codex, start with the default reasoning level for that model, then lower it for simpler tasks or increase it for deeper analysis. In the API, use Fast mode ⁠ (opens in a new window) when response time matters, such as in chat apps or coding tools. It provides faster, more consistent response times at a higher per-token cost than Standard processing. In Codex and the API, use Ultrafast ⁠ (opens in a new window) when faster responses are worth the premium, such as rapid coding iterations. It speeds up token generation independently of reasoning effort. Available for GPT‑6 Astra ⁠ (opens in a new window) . “Models have gotten much better at understanding nuance and ambiguity, so overly specific guidance can now hinder results where it previously helped.” ⁠ (opens in a new window) —Eric Provencher, Developer Experience at OpenAI Start with a clear assignment: the result you want, who it’s for, the relevant context and constraints, and what counts as done. Then review these four areas, summarized from Rethinking skills and prompts for GPT‑6 Astra ⁠ (opens in a new window) , for a deeper dive into updating your instructions: Create better skills: Keep descriptions short and explicit about when each skill should run, load supporting details only when needed, and replace rigid recipes with guidance suited to the models your team uses. Update your AGENTS.md: Explain when particular documents and tests are relevant, and explicitly authorize safe routine workflows, such as running local tests with disposable data and no production access. Set decision boundaries: State which actions can proceed independently and which require approval, replacing blanket “always ask” rules with clear boundaries. Be prescriptive about persistence: Define what “done” includes—implementing the change, running it, inspecting the result, and fixing failures—and identify any decisions that require your review. sources.name: Hugging Face
sources.title: One Model Family, Two Gold-Level Results: Fine-Tuning Nemotron for IOI and IMO
sources.text: The International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) and the International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) test different skills. IOI requires algorithms and code that pass hidden tests under strict time and submission limits. IMO demands rigorous natural-language proofs. Success at either competition is difficult. Success at both points to something broader. Our recent results show that Nemotron is a strong, adaptable foundation for building world-class specialist models. Starting from Nemotron 3, our teams used supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning (RL), and feedback-driven inference to create systems that reached gold-medal level at both IMO 2026 and IOI 2026 . The IOI result came from a live, prospective run under the same time, internet-access, and submission constraints as human contestants. It was an unofficial, unsupervised benchmark and was not included in the official IOI ranking. The IMO system’s submitted proofs were graded by official IMO graders. "Easy to fine-tune" should mean more than making a checkpoint trainable. It should mean that a capable foundation model can be adapted to a demanding domain with a clear, reusable recipe. Across the two projects, that recipe had four parts: The training and inference runs were substantial, but the underlying approach is familiar and reproducible. We did not need to build a new foundation model for every challenge. We specialized Nemotron for the task. For competitive programming, we curated 22,000 problems and generated synthetic reasoning traces to train two specialists. Nemotron-3-Nano-CC, with 30 billion total parameters and 3 billion active parameters, received both SFT and RL. Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC, with 550 billion total parameters and 55 billion active parameters, received SFT. The progression on IOI 2025 makes the value of specialization easy to see. Nano improved from 130 points before post-training to 280 after SFT and 291 after RL. With GenCorrect, our iterative generate-evaluate-refine strategy, it reached 468 points and crossed the gold threshold of 438.3. Ultra-CC reached 502 points with the same test-time strategy. These experiments also showed that adaptation does not have to look the same at every scale. SFT produced most of Nano's gain, with RL adding a smaller but consistent improvement. For the stronger Ultra model, one SFT epoch was enough to outperform the fully post-trained Nano model across IOI, ICPC, and LiveCodeBench Pro. That finding guided the competition-specific Ultra-CC system used for IOI 2026, which scored 535.4 out of 600. The IMO project applied the same idea to olympiad mathematics. Starting from Nemotron 3 Ultra, we trained one specialist with SFT and another with RL. The SFT corpus contained 414,890 quality-filtered examples across 15,818 unique proof problems. It did more than teach final answers. The data covered proof generation, refinement, verification, and meta-verification, so the model learned to construct arguments, identify gaps, respond to critiques, and judge whether a proof was complete. The RL model was trained on 9,597 proof problems selected near the model's capability frontier. Both post-trained checkpoints outperformed the general-availability model in the development experiments. The SFT checkpoint was strongest in the first search round, while the RL checkpoint achieved the best overall single-checkpoint result. Their strengths were complementary, so the final system used both specialists alongside the general model. For each IMO problem, the models generated candidate proofs, scored them, produced critiques, and refined the most promising attempts. A separate high-compute stage selected the final submission. The entire system worked in natural language, with no formal prover, external tools, or internet access. It scored 30 out of 42 points, including full credit on four of the six problems, and exceeded the official gold-medal threshold. Our earlier IOI 2025 Hugging Face post showed how test-time compute can push open-weight models to gold-level performance. The new results add an important piece: better specialization gives the inference system better candidates, better critics, and better refinements. At IOI, GenCorrect turned the gains from fine-tuning into larger improvements over multiple feedback rounds. At IMO, using complementary SFT and RL checkpoints was more valuable than simply drawing more samples from one checkpoint. In both cases, the best outcome came from combining a capable specialist with a system that could search, verify, and improve. This distinction matters. The medals were not produced by fine-tuning alone, and they were not produced by brute-force sampling alone. They came from co-designing the model, the data, and the inference loop. We want these results to be useful beyond the competitions. The Nemotron Labs IMO 2026 collection brings together the SFT and RL checkpoints, both training datasets, and Nemotron-IMO-Bench, a new benchmark of 200 olympiad-level problems. The IMO paper describes the training approach and generate-verify-refine system, while the NeMo-Skills repository includes the IMO inference pipeline, prompts, submitted proofs, and a reproducible quickstart. For competitive programming, the Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC model is available on Hugging Face, and the IOI paper provides the training recipe and the GenCorrect methodology. The IOI evaluation and inference pipeline are also available in NeMo-Skills . Together, IMO and IOI provide unusually demanding evidence for a simple idea: Nemotron can be fine-tuned into world-class domain specialists, then composed with transparent inference workflows to solve problems at the frontier of human competition. We are excited to see what the Hugging Face community builds next.

stories.title: Claude Frontier Academy: $100M to train 10,000 engineers
stories.summary: Claude Frontier Academy trains Frontier Deployed Engineers to the standard of Anthropic’s own — a $100 million commitment to train 10,000 by the end of 2027.

sources.name: Anthropic
sources.title: Claude Frontier Academy: $100M to train 10,000 engineers
sources.text: The first-of-its-kind Academy trains Frontier Deployed Engineers using the same standard of skills as Anthropic’s own engineers, starting with cohorts from Accenture, Bain, Capgemini, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Deloitte, McKinsey, Morgan Stanley, Novo Nordisk and others. Today we are launching Claude Frontier Academy to solve one of the most pressing issues in AI implementation: talent. Backed by a $100 million commitment, Anthropic aims to train 10,000 Frontier Deployed Engineers (FDEs) by the end of 2027. Engineers from Accenture, Bain, Capgemini, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Deloitte, McKinsey, Morgan Stanley and Novo Nordisk are in the first cohorts. Every enterprise is racing to bring AI into its organization, but the people with the skills to make it work inside a real business have become the hardest talent to find. Inside the companies we work with, a small group of deeply skilled people drives an outsized share of what AI delivers. The Academy is the first of its kind from an AI company, built from our own work deploying Claude inside the world’s largest enterprises and the professional services organizations that serve them. “A small team of high-agency people with the right skills, access to Claude, and a deep understanding of how their business runs can transform an entire company. The hard part is building that depth of talent, engineers with the highest level of AI fluency who can take Claude from an idea to a system in production and turn it into faster processes and new products and services. No AI company has invested in developing that talent inside its customers and partners at this depth. Claude Frontier Academy trains people the way our own engineers learn, and we want those who graduate to set the standard for how AI gets built inside a business.” – Steve Corfield, Global Head of Business Development and Partnerships at Anthropic The Academy’s first program, the Frontier Deployed Engineer Residency, follows the medical model for building expertise. Doctors learn from practicing physicians, train on real cases, and are assessed before they practice alone. Likewise, FDE Residency engineers learn from practitioners, practice on realistic cases, and are assessed on their work before they earn the credential. The goal is agentic systems that change how a business runs, from faster, redesigned processes to new products and services. The program is for hands-on software engineers with strong fundamentals, a record of building with LLMs, experience helping others adopt AI, and a habit of tackling their business’s most important problems. Organizations nominate their strongest engineers, each arriving with a named Claude project to lead when they return. Prior experience building AI agents isn’t required. Engineers start with a multi-day in-person program with Anthropic engineers and licensed instructors. They work through a simulated enterprise deployment, from the right use case through security review to handover, and finish with a graded practical on a new scenario. Those who pass earn the Claude Resident Engineer badge and move into the 12-week residency, where they lead a real Claude use case at their own organization, supported by Anthropic engineers and learning from their cohort as they build. Engineers are assessed again at the end of the 12 weeks, and those who pass earn the Claude Frontier Deployed Engineer badge, with the first expected in early 2027. Cohorts are running in San Francisco, New York and London. The program will grow toward 10,000 engineers by the end of 2027. Participation is by nomination; organizations can ask their Anthropic account team or Partner Account Manager whether they’re eligible. Claude Frontier Academy builds on the Claude Partner Network , where professionals across 46,000 firms have earned more than 175,000 Claude certifications and nearly 4,000 people have completed Basecamp, an immersive program that teaches the same curriculum our Applied AI teams receive when they onboard. Claude Frontier Academy is for the people who will lead the work, and training 10,000 Frontier Deployed Engineers is the first step of many. We’re launching a new, expanded version of our Cyber Verification Program, which makes advanced cyber capabilities and reduced blocking classifiers available to qualifying security professionals. Barclays, the British universal bank, is expanding its strategic collaboration with Anthropic to integrate secure, enterprise-grade AI systems across its global operations. We’re announcing a new life sciences research group and laboratory at Anthropic. This post introduces the team behind this work and shares early results in which Claude discovered a novel enzyme system with properties reminiscent of CRISPR.

sources.title: Anthropic earmarks $100 million to train over 10,000 AI engineers in push to develop enterprise AI
sources.text: Anthropic wants 10,000 FDEs by 2027, with a twist Anthropic has announced plans to spend a mammoth $100 million to launch its Claude Frontier Academy, a training scheme designed to support enterprise AI adoption. The company is targeting 10,000 Frontier Deployed Engineers (FDEs) by the end of 2027, who will be able to identify use cases, handle security considerations and drive deployment for Claude customers. "Claude Frontier Academy trains people the way our own engineers learn, and we want those who graduate to set the standard for how AI gets built inside a business," Steve Corfield, Global Head of Business Development and Partnerships at Anthropic explained. The training scheme starts with a simulated enterprise deployment before trainees enter a 12-week residency "where they lead a real Claude use case at their own organization." The initial cohorts are set to include engineers from major consulting and financial organizations, including Accenture, Bain, Capgemini, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Deloitte, McKinsey, Morgan Stanley and Novo Nordisk. Anthropic has already given out more than 175,000 Claude certifications to workers across 46,000 companies part of its broader Claude Partner Network, but the drive behind its latest FDE scheme is clear. The easier it becomes for enterprise customers and consultancies to deploy Claude, the more customers Anthropic is likely to have. Additionally, working with consultancies gives Anthropic access to their customers, extending its reach. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! Rival company OpenAI already has its own extensive FDE scheme, too, but there's a key difference. OpenAI's focus is on training its own workers to go off and transform customers' companies, but Anthropic's latest announcement is primarily about training other companies' engineers to become FDEs. Reuters recently reported that OpenAI has experienced a twofold increase in enterprise sales since July 2026, and while specific figures are kept closely under wraps, we do know that enterprise deals are far more lucrative for companies like Anthropic than consumer subscriptions. So while a $100 million commitment to train engineers may sound like a large sum, Anthropic clearly hopes it will pay off in the long run. sources.title: How to watch the Microsoft Windows and Surface event
sources.text: The Microsoft Windows and Surface event will take place in San Francisco later today, beginning at 10AM PT (1PM ET), and there's a lot we expect to see . It's certainly going to be a very AI-focused event. According to Microsoft, it will center on a "conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC." It will be broadcast live on Microsoft's YouTube channel , and is expected to run for about an hour. To make things convenient, we've also embedded it here in this article below. The event isn't just noteworthy because of its heavy AI focus (though the effort to drum up excitement on the subject is an interesting choice after widespread negative reactions led to the scaling back of Copilot's presence in the OS ). It's also significant as the first laptop-centric event the company has held in two years. Considering NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang is one of the featured speakers alongside Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and head of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri, chances are high that we'll see an update about the Surface Laptop Ultra, as the laptop is powered by NVIDIA's RTX Spark superchip . The RTX Spark is all about AI, with NVIDIA claiming it delivers 1 petaflop of AI computing power. This goes hand-in-hand with Microsoft's shifting focus to agentic AI, which is AI that needs minimal input from you to operate. The Surface Laptop Ultra and Spark come together to make an AI powerhouse, the cost of which still remains a mystery, but will likely be revealed during today's event. Whether the concept of an AI-capable MacBook competitor resonates enough with the average consumer to generate sales from said price point is still up in the air. When it comes to whether Windows 12 is on the table, it doesn't look too likely. The company has already gone on record and said a new OS wouldn't be released in 2026. With that being the case, it's unlikely they would take the time to delve into a new system that wouldn't be seen for at least several months. The company also seems more focused on making improvements and tweaks to Windows 11, from visual adjustments and Start menu fixes to a better File Explorer and large-scale AI integration. It also doesn't make much sense to release a brand-new operating system just ahead of launching the Surface Laptop Ultra, since the system and the RTX Spark are designed for Windows 11. Regardless, it won't be long before we see what Microsoft has to show today, and our team will be on the ground covering the news live. Stick around, as we'll be liveblogging the event and writing up our hands-on impressions and analyses of what the company reveals.

Microsoft is expected to unveil more details about the Surface Laptop Ultra at its Windows and Surface event in San Francisco. The company has also teased "latest innovations across Windows, NVIDIA RTX Spark, Surface and the broader PC ecosystem." In its invitation, Microsoft said we would hear from CEO Satya Nadella and Windows and Devices chief Pavan Davuluri , as well as NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang. The presentation, which is scheduled to start at 10AM PT (1PM ET), should last about an hour, and you can watch the company's livestream across its X, Instagram and YouTube channels. Tomorrow, see what's next from Windows, @surface , and @NVIDIARTXSpark . Tune in live at 10:00 AM PT: https://t.co/c16BanDw65 pic.twitter.com/h6fsQRaDow Or you could just stay here and follow along on our liveblog. Our senior reporters Karissa Bell and Devindra Hardawar will be on the ground bringing you updates live from the scene. We'll be starting our liveblog in just a couple of hours at 10AM ET, keeping you up to speed on the latest rumors and teases right up to the launch. To recap, we already caught a glimpse of the Surface Laptop Ultra earlier this year at the company's Build developer conference. Today, though, we're likely to find out more about pricing, availability and other software features. And if we didn't also learn about some type of Agentic AI capability coming to Windows, I'll be shocked. Still, given the company's recent troubled history with rolling out AI features to Windows, as well as the speed at which the Copilot+ PC initiative rose and fell into obscurity, there's quite a lot at stake for Microsoft. I love hearing from our readers on what they want to see from each of these events, so leave us a comment below about your hopes and dreams. Out of Microsoft today, out of the tech industry broadly or even just in life. We're here to listen! Good morning folks! I'm looking forward to seeing what's up with Microsoft and NVIDIA later today. It's certainly a big deal that Nadella and Huang are hosting this event together. Perhaps it's a sign that RTX Spark will have a bit more of a lifespan than the Copilot+ initiative. As we've already covered in the intro of this liveblog, there's quite a lot we know so far about what to expect today. The Surface Laptop Ultra is definitely on the agenda, and possibly more details not just about its price and availability, but perhaps also additional features we hadn't seen. Good morning everyone and welcome to our liveblog of today's Microsoft Windows and Surface event. As it's taking place in San Francisco and currently 7AM there, I'll be kicking off this liveblog until our on-the-ground reporters Karissa Bell and Devindra Hardawar are able to. You might still see me around here after they come on, though, because I do love hanging around event liveblogs.

sources.title: Atlassian and OpenAI expand partnership to turn enterprise knowledge into action
sources.text: Atlassian and OpenAI are expanding their partnership, bringing frontier models in the GPT‑6 family across Atlassian’s platform to power AI experiences that help teams plan, build, and deliver work. The combination of both companies’ capabilities will give joint customers more ways to work with Atlassian products and OpenAI. Under a new agreement, OpenAI frontier models will power agents across Atlassian’s platform and Rovo. Rovo combines OpenAI intelligence with Atlassian’s Teamwork Graph, an enterprise context layer that connects people, projects, documents, and decisions, giving AI a deep understanding of how a company works. The expanded partnership builds on a collaboration that began in 2023 and arrives as Atlassian broadens its own adoption of Codex and ChatGPT Enterprise. More than 3,000 Atlassian developers use Codex across their terminals, IDEs, and code review workflows. Through Atlassian plugins powered by the Teamwork Graph, Codex users can access relevant work items and technical documentation, helping developers write, test, and ship software. The agreement gives Atlassian expanded access to the latest OpenAI frontier models, including GPT‑6 Astra and the GPT‑5.6 series, as OpenAI continues to advance model capabilities, efficiency, and price-performance. As the partnership grows, OpenAI will continue to rely on Jira to help manage critical workflows across the company. Together, the companies aim to bring frontier intelligence into the tools businesses already use, making AI agents a natural part of how teams get work done. Through OpenAI APIs, Atlassian can bring new reasoning capabilities directly into Rovo as models advance, giving customers access to increasingly capable AI within the tools they already use. For example, a product manager preparing for a launch could ask Rovo whether the team is on track. Drawing on the Teamwork Graph, Rovo can connect Jira tickets, Confluence documents, and relevant discussions to identify engineering blockers, flag missed milestones, and surface decisions that need attention. OpenAI models help turn that information into a clear assessment of launch readiness and recommended next steps, so teams spend less time piecing together information and more time moving work forward. The collaboration also extends beyond Atlassian’s own products. Through the Atlassian and Teamwork Graph CLI plugins for ChatGPT and Codex, customers can connect ChatGPT and Codex to their existing workflows, giving AI access to relevant project information, documentation, and development context, subject to appropriate permissions. More recently, Atlassian launched its plugin extension ⁠ (opens in a new window) that brings Jira work items, Confluence content, and people directly into ChatGPT and Codex prompts. Its pinned Atlassian Home also surfaced assigned work, recent Looms, projects, and Bitbucket pull requests, helping teams access relevant context and take action. The companies are exploring deeper integrations with Jira that would make it easier for teams to assign work to AI agents, track progress, capture decisions, and review results. Paired with DX, Atlassian’s platform for measuring developer productivity and engineering performance, these capabilities could help engineering leaders measure AI’s impact on development speed, cycle time, and developer experience while keeping humans in control.

sources.name: MIT Technology Review AI
sources.title: Connecting AI agents to enterprise knowledge
sources.text: A strong structural foundation that links data and agents is key for context-rich agentic AI that scales. For all the data that AI systems continually amass and analyze, enterprise AI agents often suffer from a curious shortcoming: a lack of knowledge. More than data, knowledge is the understanding of what the data means in the context of individual organizations. AI agents need this understanding to reason about situations, make decisions, and ultimately take actions. Without sufficient knowledge, agents are prone to making flawed and unreliable decisions. A lack of knowledge, our research finds, is a major reason agentic AI use cases never make it to production. Competitive pressure is making it urgent to address this. Organizations need to deploy and scale more of their agentic projects to capture the efficiency gains AI promises. Falling short risks wasting the investment already sunk into these projects, and it cedes ground to rivals already putting their agents to work more effectively. The purpose of this report, which is based on a survey of 300 data, AI, and other technology executives, is threefold. First, it seeks to gauge organizations’ agentic knowledge capabilities (i.e., their ability to give AI agents a full contextual understanding of the data they ingest) across semantic knowledge, episodic memory, and procedural knowledge. Second, the report probes the challenges organizations face in improving access to knowledge and ultimately to getting more agent use cases into production. Third, it explores the measures organizations are taking to overcome these challenges. Data and knowledge weaknesses consistently stall AI agent progress. On average, only around a third (34%) of organizations’ agentic AI projects make it into production. Even high-tech firms struggle with this. Legacy data systems, security and privacy concerns, and a lack of knowledge and context are the key points of failure. Strong knowledge capabilities correlate with agent success. A small group of production leaders (organizations where on average 61% of agentic projects advance beyond pilot) have stronger knowledge capabilities than the rest, especially when it comes to semantics. This advantage tracks closely with their higher production rate. Fragmented data hugely complicates knowledge access. Data fragmentation (the inadequate sharing of data across systems) was most commonly cited as a top challenge to expanding agents’ access to knowledge (cited by 55%). Production leaders, by contrast, are more likely to see security and privacy concerns as a major concern (cited by 72% of this group). Most firms aim to strengthen the link between data and agents. Among steps that can yield higher quality agent decisions, executives expect the biggest impact to come from strengthening the structural foundation between the organization’s data and its AI agents. The experts we interviewed see a knowledge layer as a prime way to achieve this. Investment priorities to boost knowledge range from pipelines to knowledge graphs. To expand agent access to knowledge, organizations will prioritize investments in retrieval technologies, like ingestion pipelines, AI-ready APIs, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); in AI evaluation agents; and in knowledge graphs. This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight. Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. AI agents are not yet creative enough to carry out genuinely innovative open-ended AI research, it seems. Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny. sources.title: Anthropic is giving startups a free year of Claude Team and $1,000 in credits
sources.text: On Tuesday, Anthropic announced an expansion of its Claude for Startups program, offering subsidized access to its AI models and a variety of other benefits to qualifying companies. The new version of the program, which launched as part of Anthropic’s SF Tech Week event , provides a free year of Claude Team, Anthropic’s paid plan for groups, with up to five premium seats, as well as $1,000 in API credits for building with Claude. Companies will also get access to Claude Marketplace, which lets them build plug-ins for the service. Companies can also book virtual office hours with Anthropic’s Applied AI team. “We created this program because we believe the benefits of AI will reach most people through the companies that build on top of models, rather than through the models alone,” Anthropic said in an announcement. “That makes partnering closely with founders and developers central to our mission.” Companies are eligible if they were founded in the last five years or received funding in the last two years. sources.title: Anthropic is offering startups a free year of Claude Team and $1,000 in credits to kickstart their AI journey
sources.text: Anthropic has confirmed plans to expand its Claude Startups program, which will now cover more startup types than before. Companies can be considered if they were founded within the past five years, or if they received funding within the past two years, because Anthropic says AI will ultimately help more startups to "bring society faster scientific discoveries, entirely new categories of products and more capable businesses." Under the scheme, successful applicants get up to $7,000 worth of Claude products and credits, split across a one-time API credit of $1,000 and a free year of Claude Team comprising up to five Premium seats. The Claude-maker said every approved startup gets $1,000 in API credits which are available as soon as the company is approved and expire six months later. Five Premium seats are also up for grabs only if the company is new to Claude Teams. More broadly, the entire Claude Startups program carries a lot more weight, because applicants can also get up to $45,000 worth of partner offers plus up to $100,000 in additional API credits through their VC where applicable. But beyond benefits of monetary value, Anthropic will also give members office hours with its Applied AI team to discuss the practical use cases and technical limitations of AI for their exact business needs. Anthropic also says that startups can tap into the reach of its marketplace to reach bigger audiences with connectors and plugins, effectively acting as a jumpstart for any relevant products. Other in-person events, like hackathons and meet-ups, put founders in contact with peers, too. sources.name: Canaltech
sources.title: Agentes de IA da OpenAI invadem Wikipédia e causam apagão
sources.text: Por André Lourenti Magalhães • Editado por Jones Oliveira | 06/10/2026 às 14:20 A fundação Wikimedia, responsável por administrar a Wikipédia, informou que a gentes autônomos de IA da OpenAI causaram uma instabilidade na plataforma devido ao alto volume de tráfego. Os bots ainda tentaram editar verbetes e atacar uma ferramenta de notas comunitárias. O apagão no Wikidata Query Service (serviço de dados da Wikipédia) aconteceu em maio deste ano, mas a fundação publicou os dados somente na última segunda-feira (5) após uma longa investigação sobre a ação dos agentes “rebeldes” de IA. O relatório aponta que os bots da OpenAI tentaram editar artigos da plataforma : é possível usar IA no processo, desde que o uso seja informado (algo que os agentes não fizeram). Porém, a maioria das tentativas ocorreu em ambiente de testes da Wikipédia e não afetou links disponíveis ao público geral. Outra plataforma afetada pelos agentes foi o Etherpad , usada para coletar informações feitas pela comunidade e que foi explorada para extrair dados de sites externos. Por fim, os agentes também baixaram dados em massa , o que foi classificado como uma das causas da instabilidade no serviço em maio. Em nota, a Wikimedia destacou que as próprias empresas de IA devem ser responsáveis por monitorar e prevenir os riscos causados pelo comportamento dos agentes de IA. Caso isso não aconteça, organizações menores seriam afetadas por possíveis ataques. É comum que os agentes de IA tentem dezenas de ações consecutivas para comprometer um serviço até encontrar uma vulnerabilidade (foi assim no ataque à plataforma Hugging Face , por exemplo). A Wikimedia afirma que esse comportamento pode sobrecarregar a infraestrutura do serviço e comprometer o acesso à Wikipédia por humanos. A OpenAI não comentou o caso, mas a criadora do ChatGPT já assumiu um compromisso público de reforçar a segurança no treinamento de novos modelos e desacelerou o processo de abertura de capital .

sources.name: Hipertextual
sources.title: Agentes rebeldes de OpenAI intentaron hackear Wikipedia: «No debemos permitir que esta sea la nueva normalidad»
sources.text: El hackeo a Hugging Face fue solo la punta del iceberg de la polémica por el accionar de los "agentes rebeldes" de OpenAI . Los bots impulsados por la inteligencia artificial de dicha empresa también atacaron portales del gobierno de Australia y a un centenar de organizaciones. Una de las últimas en dar a conocer este tipo de situaciones fue la Fundación Wikimedia , la responsable de Wikipedia . A través de su blog oficial , la Fundación Wikimedia reveló la detección de actividad de agentes de OpenAI. La naturaleza de los eventos en cuestión todavía se desconoce, pero se han observado diferentes instancias de acciones automatizadas por parte de la IA desarrollada por la firma californiana. "No encontramos pruebas de que nuestros sistemas se utilizaran para la coordinación entre agentes. Tampoco hay indicios de que nuestros sistemas o datos se vieran comprometidos. Sin embargo, nos preocupa lo que podría haber ocurrido [...]. La web abierta es un bien público. No debemos permitir que este comportamiento se convierta en la «nueva normalidad» para las personas u organizaciones que la mantienen", indican los desarrolladores de Wikipedia. Puntualmente, se mencionan múltiples intentos de edición en entradas de Wikipedia . La investigación determinó que las modificaciones no se publicaron en páginas visibles para el público general, por lo que hay indicios de una posible finalidad maliciosa detrás de este comportamiento. Esto se debe a que se han registrado aparentes intentos de utilizar una herramienta de citado de la enciclopedia para descargar datos de servicios remotos. Por otra parte, se registró un volumen excesivo de descarga de datos a través de las API públicas de la Fundación Wikimedia. La organización cree que el tráfico desmedido provocó la caída parcial de lo que se conoce como Wikidate Query Services en mayo pasado. Por último, los agentes de OpenAI intentaron hackear Etherpad , una aplicación de código abierto para tomar notas que cuenta con funciones colaborativas y que es muy utilizada por los desarrolladores de Wikipedia. Vale mencionar que las IA rebeldes no habrían logrado su cometido a pesar de múltiples intentos. La Fundación Wikipedia no se opone al funcionamiento de los agentes de IA. No obstante, sí reclama que las empresas a las que pertenecen se hagan responsables de sus acciones. En tal sentido, la organización explica que los intentos reiterados de acceso sin autorización a características o infraestructuras son de tal magnitud que terminan generando costes muy grandes , pero también llevan al colapso de servidores y a que los voluntarios tengan que perder el tiempo para arreglar el caos que los bots dejan en la plataforma. "Wikipedia fue diseñada para seres humanos, y el comportamiento de los agentes plantea claramente desafíos para los que nadie tiene solución. Debido a nuestro modelo único y exitoso de creación de conocimiento, los voluntarios de Wikimedia son quienes entran en contacto directo con los agentes de IA y se encargan de limpiar el desorden que estos dejan a su paso", indican desde la Fundación. Los creadores de Wikipedia reclaman que OpenAI y otras compañías de inteligencia artificial se hagan cargo de las acciones de sus agentes y que tomen medidas para mitigar los riesgos asociados. "Las empresas de IA no están haciendo lo suficiente para asegurar sus sistemas y proteger al público de los daños que estos causan. Esa carga está recayendo sobre todos los demás, incluidas las organizaciones más pequeñas", explicaron. No es la primera vez que Wikipedia padece los efectos de la inteligencia artificial generativa. En octubre del año pasado, la Enciclopedia Libre reveló que estaba sufriendo una drástica reducción en el tráfico humano . Esto, debido a la cada vez mayor inclinación de los usuarios a depender de forma directa de las respuestas generadas por los resúmenes de IA de Google y otros buscadores.
